lines: January the third, two thousand and nine.
The first Bitcoin block is mined, and an ordinary laptop is enough to win the reward.
Seventeen years later, the network makes about a thousand quintillion guesses every second.
Laptops gave way to graphics cards, and then to warehouses of purpose-built chips.
For a small miner at home, the chance of winning a single block is now about one in sixteen thousand a year.
And yet, solo miners still won twenty-two blocks in twenty twenty-five.
Every block also carries a quiet fingerprint of whoever built it:
which header bits their machines roll, and how they fill the block.
We mined all nine hundred and seventy-five thousand blocks to ask three questions.
Can behaviour alone reveal who mined a block?
Does the data rediscover the eras of mining?
And should a miner in Hong Kong join a pool, gamble solo, or switch off?
